questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: identify the product law for logarithms from the shape of an expression
questions.stem: The expression 2 times the logarithm of 3 plus 3 times the logarithm of 5 is to be written as one single logarithm. Which law does the job?

options.text: the product law, because a sum of logarithms is the logarithm of a product, giving the logarithm of 9 times 125
the quotient law, because a difference of logarithms is the logarithm of a ratio, and no difference is present here
options.misconception: invokes the quotient law on an expression whose terms are being added, not subtracted

options.text: the power law, because a coefficient in front of a logarithm is absorbed into the base
options.misconception: mistakes a coefficient in front of the logarithm for an exponent inside it

options.text: the inverse law, because the two logarithms must first be undone by an exponential before anything else
options.misconception: insists on removing both logarithms before using a law that already applies to them

questions.explanation: The product law says the sum of the logarithms of two positive numbers is the logarithm of their product, and it is the only one of the three laws whose left side is a sum. The power law is needed as well here, and it handles the coefficients: 2 of the logarithm of 3 is the logarithm of 3 squared, that is the logarithm of 9, and 3 of the logarithm of 5 is the logarithm of 5 cubed, that is the logarithm of 125. With both logarithms now in the form the product law wants, the total is the logarithm of 9 times 125, which is the logarithm of 1125. Note the order of operations: the coefficients are converted to exponents first, because a sum of two logs is not directly a product law application until each term is a single logarithm of a single argument.
questions.hint: First turn each coefficient into an exponent using the power law; only then can the product law combine the sum.

questions.learningObjective: recover the argument of a condensed logarithmic expression
questions.stem: A single number N has logarithm equal to 2 times the logarithm of 3 plus 3 times the logarithm of 5. What is the value of N?
questions.explanation: The coefficients become exponents by the power law, so the expression is the logarithm of 3 squared plus the logarithm of 5 cubed. The product law then makes the whole thing one logarithm, of 3 squared times 5 cubed. Evaluating, 3 squared is 9 and 5 cubed is 125, and 9 times 125 is 1125. A second route runs the laws in the opposite direction: the prime factorisation of 1125 is 3 to the power 2 times 5 to the power 3, which is precisely the form the logarithms name, so the logarithm of 1125 must expand to 2 of the logarithm of 3 plus 3 of the logarithm of 5. That the prime exponents of the argument come out as the coefficients of the logarithms is not a coincidence; it is the whole reason this style of manipulation works, and it is the fastest route for any integer built from small primes.
questions.hint: The coefficients are prime exponents: N = 3 to the power 2 times 5 to the power 3.

there is no error, since a sum of logarithms is by definition the logarithm of the sum of the arguments

options.text: the correct value is the logarithm of 27 minus 8, which is 19, using the difference version of the law
options.misconception: uses the quotient law with a difference, which would divide the arguments rather than subtract

questions.stem: Write 2 times the logarithm of x minus 3 times the logarithm of y as one single logarithm, and state the restriction that must hold for x and y.

options.text: the logarithm of x squared over y cubed, which requires x > 0 and y > 0
the logarithm of x squared times y cubed, which requires x > 0 and y > 0

options.text: the logarithm of x squared, all minus y cubed, which requires x > 0 and y > 0
options.misconception: leaves the expression as a difference of terms instead of combining them into one logarithm

options.text: the logarithm of x squared over y, all cubed, which requires x > 0 and y > 0
options.misconception: scales the entire quotient by the coefficient instead of scaling only the second argument

The quotient law then makes a difference of logarithms into a single logarithm of a ratio, which here is the logarithm of x squared divided by y cubed. the logarithm of 2 x equals the logarithm of 2 plus the logarithm of x, by the product law
the logarithm of x divided by 2 equals the logarithm of x minus 2

questions.learningObjective: state the change-of-base formula and explain why it removes the base
questions.stem: A logarithm to a base such as 7 is rarely available on a calculator. What does the change-of-base formula give, and why is it valid?

options.text: the logarithm of a to base b equals the logarithm of a to base 10 divided by the logarithm of b to base 10, a ratio that cancels the unknown base
the logarithm of a to base b equals the logarithm of a to base 10 multiplied by the logarithm of b to base 10
options.misconception: multiplies where the formula divides, which is the reciprocal of the correct identity

options.text: the logarithm of a to base b equals the logarithm of b to base 10 divided by the logarithm of a to base 10
options.misconception: inverts the ratio, which would recover the base from the value instead of the value from the base

options.text: the logarithm of a to base b equals the ratio of the two numbers a and b taken to base 10
options.misconception: divides the arguments themselves rather than their logarithms, producing a number instead of a logarithm

The division is not a trick: the factor the logarithm of the base contributes is exactly the unknown scale of the exponential, so dividing by it is what recovers the plain exponent. The formula is numerically harmless in the other direction too, since a ratio of two logarithms to the same base is independent of which base 10 is used, so base 2 or the natural logarithm work just as well. Option C is the useful warning, because the inverted ratio is not a logarithm at all but the base that would produce the given value.

questions.learningObjective: state why exponentiating a logarithmic equation requires a back-substitution check
questions.stem: Solving a logarithmic equation usually means exponentiating both sides. Why must every candidate then be substituted back into the original equation?

options.text: exponentiating can hand back values that solve the transformed equation but sit outside the domain the logarithms required
no check is needed, because exponentiating is an invertible operation and so every candidate is automatically valid
options.misconception: assumes the algebraic step is reversible, overlooking the domain it discarded

options.text: only the sign of each candidate matters, since a negative value can flip the equation to the other side
options.misconception: believes a sign check is the whole story, when the real constraint is positivity of every argument

options.text: the check can be skipped whenever the equation has a single logarithm on each side rather than two or more
options.misconception: thinks the number of logarithms determines the need for a domain check

questions.explanation: Exponentiating is only invertible on the domain where the logarithms existed, so it silently extends the solution set of the original equation. A typical example is the equation with the logarithm of x plus 1 and the logarithm of x minus 3 equalling 1: combining gives the logarithm of the quantity x plus 1 times x minus 3, and exponentiating gives the product equal to 10. That quadratic has two roots, but the one below minus 1 makes both original arguments negative, so it solves the exponential equation and not the logarithmic one. The back-substitution is not a formality added by convention; it is the only step that restores the restriction exponentiating threw away, which is why the standard instruction is to never report a logarithmic root without testing it.
questions.hint: Exponentiating can enlarge the solution set beyond the domain the logarithms were defined on, so test each root.

questions.learningObjective: identify and discard an extraneous root produced by exponentiating

nothing is wrong, because exponentiating is reversible and both roots of the quadratic must therefore solve the original
options.misconception: treats exponentiating as reversible, ignoring the domain it discarded along the way

options.text: the larger root is the wrong one, since the product rule requires the smaller of the two arguments to come first
options.misconception: invents an ordering constraint on the arguments that the product law does not impose

options.text: both roots are extraneous, because the sum of two logarithms can never equal a positive number in this configuration
options.misconception: claims no solution exists, without checking the larger root in the original equation

The final step of any logarithmic solution must be a substitution into the original form, not into the transformed one.
questions.hint: The domain demands x greater than 3; a root below that solves only the transformed equation.

10, which is the value of the combined argument, read off without inverting the quadratic

questions.learningObjective: state the horizontal line test and why it characterises invertibility
questions.stem: A function on the real numbers has an inverse function exactly when it is one-to-one. Which graph property guarantees that, and what does it say?

options.text: the horizontal line test: no horizontal line meets the graph twice, so each output value comes from at most one input
the vertical line test: no vertical line meets the graph twice, so each input produces exactly one output
options.misconception: confuses being a function with being invertible, which are different conditions

options.text: the graph must pass through the origin, so that no translation shifts the output values away from the input
options.misconception: believes invertibility requires a fixed point at the origin

options.text: the graph must already be symmetric about the line y equals x, which only invertible functions can be
options.misconception: takes the symmetry of an inverse pair as a precondition rather than a consequence

questions.explanation: One-to-one means distinct inputs give distinct outputs, which is a statement about how outputs are shared, and that is exactly what a horizontal line probes. A horizontal line at height c picks out every input whose output equals c, so meeting the graph twice is precisely a failure of one-to-one-ness, and meeting it once or not at all is exactly what invertibility requires. The vertical line test is a different question entirely: it asks whether each input has a single output, which is the definition of being a function at all. The parabola is the standard illustration, since it passes the vertical test and fails the horizontal one on the range below its vertex, so no inverse exists there without first restricting the domain. Symmetry about the line y equals x is the consequence of having an inverse, not the precondition.
questions.hint: Invertibility is about outputs being unique, so probe the graph with lines of constant output, that is horizontal ones.

2 d for every d, since the rate of 2 applies to all distance once the firm starts charging
options.misconception: drops the flat charge and the change of rate at the breakpoint

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: distinguish constant-ratio growth from constant-difference growth
questions.stem: One population grows by the same number of individuals each year, and another keeps the same fraction of itself each year. Explain why only the second is modelled exponentially, and describe the shape of its graph.

Take the linear population. If it gains 40 individuals every year from 200, the sequence runs 200, 240, 280, 320, and each consecutive pair differs by 40. The ratios between consecutive terms are 1.2, 1.1667, 1.1429, so the multiplier changes on every step and is not constant. Now take the exponential population, which keeps a constant fraction, say a factor of 1.1 each year from 200. The sequence runs 200, 220, 242, 266.2, and each consecutive pair differs by 20, 22, 24.2, so the difference is not constant at all, while the ratio is 1.1 every single time. The same number can be described in either way for one step, which is exactly why the distinction is easy to miss, but the two descriptions diverge from the second step onward. Graphically the linear population produces a straight line, rising at a constant slope, whereas the exponential produces the familiar increasing, concave-down curve that starts shallow and steepens forever. The reason is visible in the differences: for the exponential case the gain in a year is a fixed fraction of whatever the population currently is, so once the population is larger the gain is proportionally larger too, and the gains feed on themselves. The mirror-image case is decay, where the multiplier lies between 0 and 1, the graph falls, it is concave up, and it approaches the x-axis without ever reaching it. A useful diagnostic is to ask of any data set whether the ratios of successive terms are constant or whether the differences are; the first indicates exponential behaviour and the second indicates linear.

questions.explanation: A constant difference produces a straight line and a constant ratio produces a curved, accelerating or flattening path. For the first population the successive differences are equal while the ratios drift; for the second the ratios are pinned at one value while the differences themselves grow or shrink. The two descriptions agree for a single step and diverge afterwards, which is why the distinction must be tested on more than two terms.
questions.hint: Compute both the differences and the ratios of successive terms for each population; only one of the two is constant in each case.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: explain what residual patterns reveal about a fitted model
questions.stem: A curve has been fitted to some data and the residuals are computed as observed minus predicted. Explain what the pattern of those residuals reveals about the model, and why a small total error can still hide a bad model.

answer.exemplar: A residual is the vertical gap between what the data show and what the model predicted at that same input, taken as observed minus predicted. Because that convention is fixed, a positive residual means the data sit above the curve and a negative one means they sit below, and the size of the residual measures how far off the prediction was at that point. What makes residuals informative is that they are the only part of the data the model failed to account for, so if the model were right in form as well as in parameters the residuals should look like noise: a formless horizontal band centred on zero, with no curve running through the middle of it and no tendency to fan out. Any visible structure is a message. If the residuals rise and then fall in a smooth arc, the model is systematically too low at one end and too high in the middle, which means the true relationship is curved and a straight or simple form is the wrong shape entirely. If the band of residuals widens as the predictions grow, the errors are getting larger in proportion to the size of the values, so a constant-variance assumption has failed even though the centre of the band sits on zero. If the residuals wander up and down in an alternating way, the data may have been entered in the wrong order or the errors may be correlated with each other. The reason a small total error can conceal all of this is worth stating plainly. A sum of squares is a single number, and a single number cannot show shape. A model can miss systematically in both directions, so the residuals partly cancel in the total, and the resulting small figure looks like success while the model is in fact biased. The protection is that the residuals always sum to exactly zero, whatever the model, because the least-squares line is built to pass through the point of means. So a zero total is not evidence of a good fit at all; it is guaranteed. The only informative question is whether the residuals look like structureless noise, and that is a question about the picture, not the total.

questions.explanation: Residuals are the portion of the data the model has not explained, so systematic shape in them is evidence the model is wrong in form. A small summed square error cannot detect that, because residuals on either side of the curve cancel in the total, and a zero sum of residuals is guaranteed by least squares rather than earned by a good model. The diagnostic has to be made on the shape of the residual plot, not on its total.
questions.hint: Compare what the residual pattern looks like against what a correctly specified model would produce: formless noise centred on zero.

questions.stem: Residuals are plotted against the values the model predicted. What should the picture look like if the model form is appropriate?

options.text: a formless horizontal band centred on zero, with no systematic curve and no growth in spread as predictions rise
a band that curves and then flattens, which would show the model capturing the shape of the data
options.misconception: reads a systematic curve in the residuals as evidence the model is correct

options.text: a band that widens as the predictions grow, which would show errors proportional to the values
options.misconception: accepts a widening band as harmless, when it signals non-constant variance

options.text: a narrow strip running along the diagonal, which would show that the fit reproduces the data
options.misconception: expects the residuals themselves to be large, confusing them with the data

questions.explanation: The expectation comes from what a residual is: the leftover after the model has taken everything it can. If the model form is right, those leftovers are the parts of the data that are genuinely irregular, and irregularity shows as a scatter with no discernible trend. The three properties to check are therefore a centre at zero, an absence of curve, and an absence of fanning. Each catches a different failure. A centre away from zero signals a systematic offset; a curve in the middle of the band signals the wrong functional form, since the model is systematically wrong in a direction that changes with the input; and a band that widens signals that the size of the error depends on the size of the value, so a single spread parameter no longer describes the noise. Option B is the trap that catches most students, because a visible arc looks like structure in the data when it is really structure in the failure.
questions.hint: A sound model leaves only irregular noise, so check the centre, the absence of curve, and the constancy of the spread.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: diagnose an inadequate linear model from a residual pattern
questions.stem: Data points (1,1), (2,4), (3,9), (4,16) and (5,25) are fitted with a least-squares straight line, which comes out as y = 6 x minus 7. The residuals, observed minus predicted, are 2, minus 1, minus 2, minus 1 and 2. What does this pattern show?

options.text: a symmetric bowl, positive at both ends and negative in the middle, so a straight line under-predicts the extremes and over-predicts the centre
an alternating pattern, which shows the points were entered in the wrong order along the x-axis
options.misconception: reads an alternating residual pattern as a data-entry error

options.text: no problem at all, since the residuals sum to zero the fitted line must be adequate
options.misconception: treats a zero sum of residuals as evidence of a good fit, which least squares guarantees

options.text: a widening spread, which shows the measurement error grew steadily as x increased
options.misconception: reads a change in the level of residuals as a change in their spread

questions.explanation: The predicted values from the fitted line are minus 1, 5, 11, 17 and 23, and subtracting them from the observed values 1, 4, 9, 16 and 25 gives 2, minus 1, minus 2, minus 1 and 2. Those five numbers form a shallow but unmistakable bowl: positive at both ends, negative in the middle, with the sign changing twice. A straight line that under-predicts at both extremes while over-predicting in between is exactly what a curved data set produces, since the true relationship here rises faster and faster, and the data are the squares of the inputs. The pattern is the diagnosis, and the appropriate response is a different model form rather than a re-run of the same fit. Option C is worth dwelling on, because the residuals do sum to exactly zero, and that is not a coincidence to be pleased about: every least-squares fit has this property by construction, so it carries no information whatever about adequacy.
questions.hint: Plot the residual signs against the input. Two sign changes in the same direction mean the model is the wrong shape, not merely mis-parameterised.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: order the steps of a defensible modelling cycle
questions.stem: Put these five activities into the order that produces a defensible model rather than a curve that merely fits.

options.text: Decide which quantity is to be predicted and gather the data that will be used
Choose a candidate form for the relationship, guided by the shape of the data
Fit the parameters of that form to the data by a stated procedure
Compute the residuals and inspect them for systematic structure
Report the model's range of validity instead of extending it beyond the observed data

questions.explanation: The sequence is a loop with a decision at its centre, and the order carries real methodological weight. The first two activities are commitments: a model for an unstated quantity answers nothing, and a form chosen before looking at the data will be a form imposed rather than discovered. Fitting follows, but it is only a calculation, and a calculation that produces a small error is not by itself evidence of a good model. Inspecting the residuals is what converts the fitted line from a curve into a model that has been tested, because that is the step where systematic structure becomes visible and the form is vindicated or overturned. The final activity is what a report owes the reader: the range of inputs actually observed is the range over which the relationship has any support, and a prediction outside it is a guess dressed as an output. If the residuals show structure, the honest outcome is to return to the second step with a different form.
questions.hint: Commit to the question, choose a form, fit, then test the fit against the residuals before claiming anything.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: apply a domain restriction to discard a root of a transformed equation
questions.stem: A student solves the equation with the logarithm of x plus the logarithm of the quantity x minus 8 equal to the logarithm of 6, reaches a quadratic, and reports both of its roots. What is the correct solution set?

options.text: only x = 4 plus the square root of 22, about 8.690416, since the domain demands x above 8 which the other root fails
both roots, because a quadratic supplies two values and a logarithmic system inherits both of them
options.misconception: counts the roots of a quadratic without applying the domain restriction

options.text: only x = 4 minus the square root of 22, about minus 0.690416, since the smaller root lies nearer the origin
options.misconception: prefers the smaller root on grounds unrelated to the domain

options.text: no solution, because a product of two arguments can never equal 6 for values of x above 8
options.misconception: denies that any value in the domain can satisfy the equation

questions.explanation: The two logarithms require both arguments to be positive, so x must exceed 0 and x minus 8 must exceed 0, and the binding condition is x above 8. The equation combines to the logarithm of the product of x and x minus 8, and exponentiating gives that product equal to 6, that is x squared minus 8 x minus 6 equal to 0. The quadratic formula gives x equal to 4 plus or minus the square root of 22, and those are 8.690416 and about minus 0.690416. Only the first exceeds 8, so it is the sole solution, and substitution confirms it since 8.690416 times 0.690416 is 6 to nine decimal places. The second root survives the product equation while failing the original, which is the standard way exponentiating enlarges the solution set and the reason a domain check is not optional.
questions.hint: The domain needs x above 8. Compute both quadratic roots, then discard any that fall outside it.
